title: Iran Walked Away From the Table. India's Oil Clock Just Started Ticking Faster.
excerpt: Tehran suspended ceasefire talks after Israel struck Tyre, the US hit Qeshm island, and global oil inventories fell toward their lowest levels since 2003.
body:
Iran has suspended ceasefire negotiations with the United States, warning of a "decisive response" to any further violations of the fragile truce — a dramatic escalation that threatens to keep the Strait of Hormuz closed well into the summer and deepen India's worst energy crisis in decades.

The walkout, announced via Iran's semi-official Tasnim News Agency on Monday evening, came hours after Israel launched its deadliest strike on the Lebanese port city of Tyre since fighting erupted in March, killing at least eight people. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi defended the suspension on social media, arguing that the proposed ceasefire was meant to cover all regional fronts.

"A violation of the peace on one front constitutes a violation on all fronts," Araghchi wrote, holding the United States and Israel "fully responsible for the ongoing consequences."

## The Apache Incident and Retaliatory Strikes

The diplomatic collapse followed a separate flashpoint earlier Tuesday, when Iran downed a US Army Apache helicopter over the Strait of Hormuz using a one-way attack drone. Both crew members were rescued after two hours by a US Navy surface drone near Oman's coast.

President Trump confirmed the shoot-down in an ABC News interview: "They shot down a helicopter, and we are responding as we speak. I believe the response should be very strong, very powerful, and that's what this one is."

The Pentagon subsequently struck targets on Iran's Qeshm island and at Sirik, both near the strait. Iran's state media confirmed projectile hits in eastern Hormozgan province, and a military source warned of a "decisive response" to any renewed "hostility by the enemy."

Despite the escalation, Trump appeared reluctant to commit to full-scale war. Speaking to reporters after Monday night's Knicks game, he laid out his calculus: "If we go and bomb — which we can do very easily — you won't have the strait open for months. A lot of people are going to be killed. Who wants to do that?"

## What This Means for India

For India, the collapse of talks is a worst-case scenario in slow motion. The Strait of Hormuz carried a fifth of the world's crude oil before the war began on February 28, and Tehran has continued to block most marine traffic even during the ceasefire.

The US Energy Information Administration warned on Tuesday that global oil inventories in OECD nations are heading toward their lowest levels since 2003, falling to just under 2.3 billion barrels by December. The EIA now expects global oil demand to decline in 2026 for the first time since the pandemic — not because the world wants less oil, but because it cannot get enough.

India's oil-and-gas import bill jumped 53% in April from March. The Reserve Bank of India responded with emergency measures last Friday — concessional forex swaps, overseas borrowing facilities, capital gains tax exemptions on government bonds — that analysts at Jefferies estimate could draw $50 billion to $70 billion in foreign inflows. The rupee strengthened 0.4% on Tuesday to 95.35 per dollar, and the Nifty Bank index surged 2.1% as markets digested the measures.

But bankers and policymakers know these are stopgaps. India cannot hedge its way out of a strait that stays shut.

## The Deal That May Not Come

Secretary of State Marco Rubio was blunt about American expectations: the strait needs to be "open, unimpeded, without tolls, and obviously that needs to happen immediately." A senior administration official outlined Trump's framework — immediate reopening of Hormuz followed by a 60-day window for nuclear talks. Iran, however, continues to insist on controlling strait traffic indefinitely.

Trump has separately floated linking any deal to broader Abraham Accords participation, adding yet another complication. For the roughly 600,000 Indian sailors who crew the world's tanker fleets, for the 10 million Indian workers in the Gulf, and for an economy that imports 85% of its crude oil, every day without a deal is a day the margin for error shrinks further.
